title: The map works; the turn doesn't
overview: Spatial reasoning research separates seeing where things are from working out a changed viewpoint, while a humanoid learns to catch using onboard vision. Predictive models guide self-improvement, purpose-built simulators train agents, and the UK AI Security Institute argues that oversight needs to start before release.
paragraphs: Good afternoon, it's 5:22 PM. Monday the twelfth of October, twenty twenty-six.

When a model gets left and right wrong, did it misread the picture, or fail to turn it round in its head? S-Space offers a way to separate those failures. The researchers track how spatial-answer scores change as they adjust internal signals representing objects. That reveals a linear workspace: readable coordinates across the image, with distance encoded too. They can read it even when the question isn't spatial. More importantly, intervening in that workspace changes spatial judgements while largely preserving other answers. That's stronger evidence than just finding a correlation.

The intriguing failure comes after perception: the model can represent locations but struggles to transform them when the viewpoint changes. Compass directions also get tangled with directions relative to the image. I'd read this for the diagnostic method. There's code, but no named model or benchmark, and no accuracy figure to tell us how broadly the claim holds. For your own stack, check whether the internal location is right before blaming the camera.

And when the object is flying towards you, a correct location isn't enough. Reflex teaches a humanoid to catch boxes by first learning whole-body control through rewards, then inferring motion from incomplete observations. Finally, a colour-and-depth camera encoder learns that motion representation while the controller stays fixed. In simulation, catches reach eighty-five point seven percent versus eighty-seven point nine with privileged box observations. The bit I'd take seriously is the removal test: losing visual history costs roughly thirty-six to forty percentage points. Motion needs a past. On a real Unitree G1, success is sixty-five percent at two point five metres, falling to forty percent at five metres. Boxes only, with no competing system tested on the hardware.

Predicting what happens next can also decide what an agent should learn. RSI-Anything uses a predictive world model to choose actions and training data, retaining updated model-policy pairs only after compatibility checks. With the coder fixed, repair success goes from twenty-six point three percent with a static verifier to thirty-one point two after world-model adaptation, at comparable test usage. Reaction optimisation reaches ninety-six point one five percent mean best observed yield against eighty-two point one six for Bayesian optimisation, which uses previous experiments to choose the next, on the same forty-experiment budget. Laboratory planning improves too; the interface-task claim is thinner. Code's available, but the base models and benchmarks aren't named. I'd borrow the retention checks before buying the self-improvement label.

That prospect of systems helping improve themselves is also becoming a governance problem. The UK AI Security Institute says release-time checks are too late: capable unreleased systems can pose risks inside development, including during evaluation itself. It says it's independently evaluated more than fifty-five models before release, and warns that benchmarks fill up faster than credible replacements arrive. Its eight best-practice priorities include lifecycle oversight and agent incident reporting, alongside independent audit and measurement of AI's contribution to development speed. These aren't mandates. My read is that internal deployment needs to be treated as a live operating environment, not a harmless waiting room for launch.

Better evaluation also needs better stand-ins for people. Microsoft Research says StudentSim specialises pooled learner data to one student: chess response fidelity reaches zero point five one five zero versus Maia two's zero point four five three five, with a separate test of responsiveness to tutor guidance; that's the lab's own account. For broader interactions, Meta's nine-billion-parameter MIMESIS learns from human conversations with explicit reasoning supervision; agents trained against it beat those trained against an assistant playing the user across all nine unseen test simulators, though absolute agent scores aren't given.

And if testing keeps finding unresolved problems, when should training stop? Writing as orthonormal, one author proposes resolving every significant alignment issue before training the next generation: pacing without a blanket pause, but the acknowledged missing definitions of 'generation' and 'resolved' need enforceable thresholds before that's an operational rule.

I'd put viewpoint changes into a spatial test before trusting a static-layout score. And if you're training against simulated people, test against a different simulator before spending the apparent gain.
